## Proof

**Definition.** The S-restricted irrationality measure is
$$\mu_S(x) = \sup\{\mu > 0 : |x - p/q| < q^{-\mu} \text{ for infinitely many } p \in \mathbb{Z},\; q \in S\}.$$

**Setup.** Let $S = \langle p_1, \ldots, p_n \rangle$ be the subgroup of $(\mathbb{Q}^+, \times)$ generated by the first $n$ primes. As a set of positive integers (denominators), $S = \{p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_n^{a_n} : a_i \geq 0\}$.

**Counting function.** The number of $S$-elements up to $Q$ is
$$N_S(Q) = \#\{q \in S : 1 \leq q \leq Q\} \sim \frac{(\log Q)^n}{n!\,\prod_{i=1}^n \log p_i} = C_n (\log Q)^n.$$
This grows polylogarithmically — slower than any power of $Q$.

---

### Upper Bound: $\mu_S(x) \leq 1$ for almost all $x$

Fix $\mu > 1$. For each $q \in S$, define the "approximation set"
$$E_q(\mu) = \{x \in [0,1] : \exists\, p \in \mathbb{Z},\; |x - p/q| < q^{-\mu}\}.$$
This is a union of at most $q+1$ intervals of length $2q^{-\mu}$, so
$$m(E_q(\mu)) \leq (q+1) \cdot 2q^{-\mu} \leq 2q^{1-\mu} = \frac{2}{q^{\mu-1}}.$$

The total measure sum over $S$ is:
$$\sum_{q \in S} m(E_q(\mu)) \leq 2\sum_{q \in S} \frac{1}{q^{\mu-1}}.$$

Since $S = \{p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_n^{a_n} : a_i \geq 0\}$, we can factor the sum:
$$\sum_{q \in S} \frac{1}{q^{\mu-1}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{a_i=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{p_i^{a_i(\mu-1)}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1 - p_i^{-(\mu-1)}} < \infty,$$
which converges because $p_i^{-(\mu-1)} < 1$ for each $i$ when $\mu > 1$.

By the **Borel–Cantelli lemma**, the set of $x \in [0,1]$ belonging to infinitely many $E_q(\mu)$ has measure zero. Taking $\mu = 1 + 1/k$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ and intersecting the resulting full-measure sets, we conclude:
$$\mu_S(x) \leq 1 \quad \text{for almost all } x.$$

---

### Lower Bound: $\mu_S(x) \geq 1$ for all $x$

For $\mu = 1$ and any $x \in [0,1]$, given any $q \in S$, let $p = \lfloor xq + 1/2 \rfloor$ (the nearest integer to $xq$). Then
$$\left|x - \frac{p}{q}\right| \leq \frac{1}{2q} < \frac{1}{q} = q^{-1}.$$

Since $S$ is infinite (it contains $\{p_1^a : a \geq 0\}$), there are infinitely many $q \in S$, yielding infinitely many distinct rationals $p/q$ (distinct because their denominators in lowest terms are unbounded). Therefore $\mu_S(x) \geq 1$ for **every** $x \in [0,1]$.

---

### Conclusion

Combining both bounds:
$$\mu_S(x) = 1 \quad \text{for almost all } x.$$

The value $\xi = 1$ is **independent of $n$** (the number of generators). The key structural reason is that any finitely generated subgroup $S$ of $(\mathbb{Q}^+, \times)$ has counting function $N_S(Q) = O((\log Q)^n)$, which grows slower than $Q^\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$. This makes the Borel–Cantelli sum $\sum_{q \in S} q^{-(\mu-1)}$ converge for **all** $\mu > 1$ (via the factorization into geometric series), regardless of $n$. The threshold sits exactly at $\mu = 1$.

This contrasts sharply with the dense case (e.g., $S = \mathbb{Q}^+$), where $N_S(Q) \sim Q$ and the classical Khintchine theory gives $\xi = 2$ for almost all $x$. The transition from dense to finitely generated collapses the measure from $2$ to $1$.

$$\boxed{\xi = 1}$$

## Proof

**Definition.** The S-restricted irrationality measure is
$$\mu_S(x) = \sup\{\mu > 0 : |x - p/q| < q^{-\mu} \text{ for infinitely many } p \in \mathbb{Z},\; q \in S\}.$$

**Setup.** Let $S = \langle p_1, \ldots, p_n \rangle$ be the subgroup of $(\mathbb{Q}^+, \times)$ generated by the first $n$ primes. As a set of positive integers (denominators), $S = \{p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_n^{a_n} : a_i \geq 0\}$.

**Counting function.** The number of $S$-elements up to $Q$ is
$$N_S(Q) = \#\{q \in S : 1 \leq q \leq Q\} \sim \frac{(\log Q)^n}{n!\,\prod_{i=1}^n \log p_i} = C_n (\log Q)^n.$$
This grows polylogarithmically — slower than any power of $Q$.

---

### Upper Bound: $\mu_S(x) \leq 1$ for almost all $x$

Fix $\mu > 1$. For each $q \in S$, define the "approximation set"
$$E_q(\mu) = \{x \in [0,1] : \exists\, p \in \mathbb{Z},\; |x - p/q| < q^{-\mu}\}.$$
This is a union of at most $q+1$ intervals of length $2q^{-\mu}$, so
$$m(E_q(\mu)) \leq (q+1) \cdot 2q^{-\mu} \leq 2q^{1-\mu} = \frac{2}{q^{\mu-1}}.$$

The total measure sum over $S$ is:
$$\sum_{q \in S} m(E_q(\mu)) \leq 2\sum_{q \in S} \frac{1}{q^{\mu-1}}.$$

Since $S = \{p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_n^{a_n} : a_i \geq 0\}$, we can factor the sum:
$$\sum_{q \in S} \frac{1}{q^{\mu-1}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{a_i=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{p_i^{a_i(\mu-1)}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{1 - p_i^{-(\mu-1)}} < \infty,$$
which converges because $p_i^{-(\mu-1)} < 1$ for each $i$ when $\mu > 1$.

By the **Borel–Cantelli lemma**, the set of $x \in [0,1]$ belonging to infinitely many $E_q(\mu)$ has measure zero. Taking $\mu = 1 + 1/k$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ and intersecting the resulting full-measure sets, we conclude:
$$\mu_S(x) \leq 1 \quad \text{for almost all } x.$$

---

### Lower Bound: $\mu_S(x) \geq 1$ for all $x$

For $\mu = 1$ and any $x \in [0,1]$, given any $q \in S$, let $p = \lfloor xq + 1/2 \rfloor$ (the nearest integer to $xq$). Then
$$\left|x - \frac{p}{q}\right| \leq \frac{1}{2q} < \frac{1}{q} = q^{-1}.$$

Since $S$ is infinite (it contains $\{p_1^a : a \geq 0\}$), there are infinitely many $q \in S$, yielding infinitely many distinct rationals $p/q$ (distinct because their denominators in lowest terms are unbounded). Therefore $\mu_S(x) \geq 1$ for **every** $x \in [0,1]$.

---

### Conclusion

Combining both bounds:
$$\mu_S(x) = 1 \quad \text{for almost all } x.$$

The value $\xi = 1$ is **independent of $n$** (the number of generators). The key structural reason is that any finitely generated subgroup $S$ of $(\mathbb{Q}^+, \times)$ has counting function $N_S(Q) = O((\log Q)^n)$, which grows slower than $Q^\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$. This makes the Borel–Cantelli sum $\sum_{q \in S} q^{-(\mu-1)}$ converge for **all** $\mu > 1$ (via the factorization into geometric series), regardless of $n$. The threshold sits exactly at $\mu = 1$.

This contrasts sharply with the dense case (e.g., $S = \mathbb{Q}^+$), where $N_S(Q) \sim Q$ and the classical Khintchine theory gives $\xi = 2$ for almost all $x$. The transition from dense to finitely generated collapses the measure from $2$ to $1$.

$$\boxed{\xi = 1}$$
